questions.question: Explain why untreated canvas is not waterproof and describe the two families of chemical treatment that waterproof a textile, with examples, their advantages and limitations, and the problem of seams.
questions.expected_answer: Canvas is tightly woven cotton whose fibres wet and swell, so rain soaks through, although the swelling closes the gaps so the wet canvas becomes nearly waterproof, slowly and heavily. The repellent family coats each fibre with a substance water cannot wet: paraffin or beeswax worked into the cloth, linseed and other oils as on oilskin, and modern silicone or fluorocarbon sprays and dips that leave an invisible repellent layer; drops bead and roll off, the weave still breathes, treatments are cheap and renewable, but they wear off with abrasion and washing and water under pressure, a pooled roof or a knee on the floor, comes through. The coating family lays a continuous film: acrylic painted on canvas, polyurethane on nylon and polyester flys, PVC laminated on polyester for truck tarpaulins, and thin plastic laminated on both sides of woven polypropylene tape for hardware shop tarpaulins; these block water completely and resist pressure but do not breathe, so condensation forms and ventilation is needed, and they crack with age and ultraviolet light. Every needle hole in a seam leaks, so seams are taped, welded or sealed, or the fabric used in one piece.

questions.question: Describe how waterproofing is tested by drip, spray and pressure tests, give the expected results for untreated, waxed, silicone-treated, acrylic-coated and PVC-coated samples, and explain the seam test.
questions.expected_answer: In the drip test the square is clamped taut over a jar with a funnel 100 millimetres above, 50 millilitres is dripped onto one spot and the time to the first drop in the jar is recorded up to five minutes with the volume collected. In the spray test the square is held at 45 degrees and sprayed ten times from 200 millimetres and scored from complete beading, through beading with surface wetting and soaking without passing, to passing through. In the pressure test the wet square is pressed on a paper towel with a thumb for ten seconds and the towel checked. Untreated canvas drips within a minute, soaks on spray and wets the towel; waxed canvas does not drip, beads with slight wetting and dampens the towel under firm pressure; silicone-sprayed canvas does not drip, beads perfectly, dampens under pressure and fails where rubbed with sandpaper; acrylic-coated canvas, PVC-coated polyester and polypropylene tarpaulin do not drip, do not wet and leave the towel dry; plastic sheet stays dry but tears at the clamp. Weight, feel and flexibility are recorded too. A seam sewn in tarpaulin leaks at every needle hole under the drip test and stops leaking when taped or sealed, which is why shelter seams must be taped, welded or sealed.

questions.question: Describe the burning characteristics of cotton, waxed cotton, polyester and nylon, PVC-coated fabric, polypropylene tarpaulin, wool and flame-retardant-treated canvas as shown in the flame demonstration, explain why they matter for a shelter, and describe how the shelter textile is chosen.
questions.expected_answer: In the teacher's demonstration with tongs over sand, each square is held edge-first in a candle for three seconds and observed for ignition, continued burning, melting and dripping, smoke and residue. Cotton catches at once, burns steadily when withdrawn and leaves soft ash; waxed cotton burns faster and hotter because wax is fuel. Polyester and nylon shrink, melt into a dripping bead that burns briefly and leave a hard black bead that would stick to skin. PVC-coated polyester is hard to ignite, chars, self-extinguishes but gives dense acrid toxic smoke. Polypropylene tarpaulin melts quickly and drips burning droplets. Wool singes, chars slowly, smells of burnt hair and goes out. Flame-retardant-treated canvas chars where touched but does not catch or spread and goes out. These matter because families will use stoves and candles inside, a melting dripping roof causes the worst burns, and smoke in a sealed shelter kills before flame. The textile is chosen from a table of samples against waterproof score, pressure resistance, breathability, ignition, melting and dripping, smoke, weight, cost and durability, weighted with safety first, then weight and cost, then breathability which ventilation can replace; most teams specify a flame-retardant-treated, waterproof-coated canvas or polyester for roof and walls and cheaper tarpaulin for the groundsheet, with the reason written down.
